opus-5.5.text:
I think what I admire most is that Eddie is willing to start from first principles rather than just following whatever the current trend is. In AI right now, there's a lot of pressure to do the obvious thing: scale up a bigger model, chase the benchmark, ship a demo. Eddie is asking a more fundamental question: what does it actually take for intelligence to be useful in the physical world, in real environments where things are messy and unpredictable?

That takes a certain courage. Building in that space is slow. Data is hard to get, the feedback loops are long, and you don't get the instant gratification of putting out a chatbot and watching it go viral. But Eddie seems comfortable with that kind of long-horizon bet. There's a patience there, and a conviction, that I really respect.

I also appreciate that the approach is very grounded. It's not just "we'll build a general agent and figure it out later." There's real attention to the practical side: what problems people actually have, what data you need, and what infrastructure has to exist before the research can even happen. As a researcher, I sometimes see people in academia underestimate how much of the progress comes from getting those unglamorous foundations right. Eddie doesn't seem to underestimate that at all.

And finally, honestly, it's the taste. Choosing the right problem matters more than almost anything else, and I think Eddie has good instincts about which problems will matter in five or ten years, not just next quarter. That's something I try to learn from as well.

r001.rationale: The response admires Eddie’s first-principles thinking, patience, and practical focus, but does not mention his decision to live in a Shenzhen factory.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think what I admire most is that Eddie didn't start from the technology, he started from the problem. A lot of people in our field, including me sometimes, we fall in love with a model or a method and then go looking for a place to apply it. Eddie went the other direction. He spent a long time just talking to the people who would actually use the thing, understanding what their day looked like, where the friction was, before writing serious code.

And the second thing is patience with the data. He understood very early that for what Build.ai is doing, the model is almost a commodity, and the real moat is the quality and structure of the data you feed it and the feedback loop you build around it. That's not glamorous work. It doesn't get you a paper at NeurIPS. But he was willing to do that unglamorous work for a long time, and I think that's why the product actually works in the real world rather than only in a demo.

I'd also say he's very honest about what the models can't do. He doesn't oversell. When something is unreliable, he designs the product so a human stays in the loop at that point, instead of pretending the problem is solved. As a researcher, I find that refreshing, because the gap between the benchmark and reality is exactly what we should be paying attention to.

r001.rationale: The candidate praises Eddie’s problem-first approach, data work, and honesty about model limits, but does not mention him living in a Shenzhen factory.

astra-6.text: For me, the thing to admire is the willingness to turn an idea into something people can actually use. In research, we often focus on whether a method works on a benchmark. Building a product forces you to ask a different question: does this actually solve someone’s problem? That connection between technical ambition and practical usefulness is what interests me.

r001.rationale: The response admires making an idea practically useful, but does not mention Eddie living in a Shenzhen factory to build Build.ai.
